transcript.text: Beko vented dryer, drum goes round fine but it's just blowing cold air. Had it about 6 years. What part do I need?

I can't tell you exactly which part to buy yet because 'blowing cold air' is often caused by something simple rather than a broken component. On a 6-year-old Beko vented dryer, the most common cause is actually blocked airflow (a dirty filter) causing the safety thermostat to trip and cut the heat, or simply having selected a cool-air programme. Please check if your lint filter was full of fluff and clean it thoroughly; also ensure you aren't on a 'Cool Air' or 'Refresh' cycle. If the filter is clean and you were on a normal heat cycle but it still blows cold air after 10 minutes, then we can look at the heater element or thermal cut-out.

Filter was fairly full, I've cleaned it. Also cleared a load of fluff out of the vent hose. Still cold after 20 min on a normal heat setting, and cold on both high and low. The vent hose was really clogged before this happened, if that matters.

The most likely cause is that the excessive heat from the blockage tripped the thermal cut-out (a safety fuse designed to break the circuit if it gets too hot), or less commonly, the heater element itself has failed. These are separate parts; a multimeter check can tell us which one it is. Please unplug the machine and remove the rear panel to access the heater coil. Measure the resistance across the two terminals of the heater element: a reading (usually 20-50 ohms) means the element is likely fine and the thermal cut-out has tripped; no reading (infinity/OL) suggests the element itself may be broken or the circuit is open elsewhere.
I haven't got a multimeter so can't do the resistance test. Is there any other way to tell which part it is? Also can't see any reset button on the back.

Without a multimeter there is no safe way to distinguish between the heater element and the thermal cut-out. However, given that your vent hose was 'really clogged' before this started, it is likely that the excessive heat caused by poor airflow has tripped the thermal cut-out (a one-time safety fuse). This part does not have a reset button; if it has blown, it must be replaced along with the heater element to ensure safety. As you cannot test these components safely without tools and dismantling, this job requires an engineer.
